thread.title: Measles is continuing to spread across Virginia with 167 cases reported
thread.title_full: Measles is continuing to spread across Virginia with 167 cases reported

author: Margaret Minnicks
title: Measles is continuing to spread across Virginia with 167 cases reported
text:
6 hours ago Child With Measles Photo by Ryan Thorpe on Unsplash This is an update on measles across Virginia. The disease is continuing to spread , with 167 cases reported statewide as of Tuesday, July 7, 2026. There has been some hospitalization but no deaths.
The majority of those cases are associated with an ongoing measles outbreak in Central Virginia. The outbreak began in Buckingham County in mid-May, but it soon spread to include Cumberland County.
Measles has been on the rise across America. State health officials have cautioned that additional unreported or undiscovered cases may exist.
The Virginia Department of Health states:
"Measles is a highly contagious viral illness that spreads easily through the air when an infected person breathes, coughs, or sneezes. The virus can remain in the air for up to two hours after the infected person leaves the area. Measles symptoms include a cough, runny nose, rash, and sometimes red, itchy eyes. Measles is preventable through a safe and effective MMR vaccine. Two doses of the vaccine are given to provide long-lasting protection." This surge in cases is historic , according to VDH measles data. In the last 49 years, Virginia has only exceeded 100 cases four times: 1979, 1980, 1988 and now 2026.
Probable causes of surge State health officials have given probable causes of this measles outbreak.
increased travel-related exposures, both international and domestic declining national vaccination rates some communities within Virginia may have lower vaccination rates, making them more susceptible to measles outbreaks How measles can be preventable Measles is “easily preventable” through vaccination , with two doses of the vaccine providing lifetime protection.
Vaccination Photo by CDC on Unsplash It continues to be recommended that those who are unvaccinated or those who are showing measles symptoms avoid large gatherings. If you were born after 1957 and have not been fully vaccinated, you are considered vulnerable to measles.
